rationale_evidence.anchor: A Dempster-Shafer state does not necessarily assign one probability to each proposition. It can represent a mass distribution over sets of possibilities ... support for a set of hypotheses rather than commitment to one hypothesis. ... S_{t+1}=U_{DS}(S_t,E). This is exactly why we need the abstract layer.
rationale_evidence.statement: Dempster-Shafer instantiates U_R differently from Bayesian: instead of P(H) it assigns mass m(A) over sets of possibilities, deriving Bel(A) and Pl(A), representing support for a set of hypotheses rather than commitment to one -- yet the abstract transition remains S_{t+1}=U_{DS}(S_t,E), which is exactly why the abstract layer is needed.

rationale_evidence.anchor: mu_overloaded(x)=0.8 ... does not automatically mean P(overloaded)=0.8. And it does not mean Knowledge(overloaded)=0.8. ... S^fuzzy_{t+1}=U_fuzzy(S_t,E). The numerical value has a completely different semantics from Bayesian probability.
rationale_evidence.statement: Fuzzy logic instantiates U_R with membership degree mu_overloaded(x)=0.8, which does not automatically mean P(overloaded)=0.8 nor Knowledge(overloaded)=0.8 -- the numerical value has a completely different semantics from Bayesian probability, yet fuzzy reasoning still fits the abstract update pattern S^fuzzy_{t+1}=U_fuzzy(S_t,E).

rationale_evidence.anchor: normally(P) and P is currently derived. Then new evidence arrives: not-P. A non-monotonic system may retract the previous consequence. So S_t={P} can become S_{t+1}={not-P}. This is not Bayesian posterior movement. It is: defeasible revision. ... U_NMR(S_t,E)->S_{t+1}.
rationale_evidence.statement: Non-monotonic reasoning instantiates U_R as defeasible revision: given normally(P) and P currently derived, new evidence not-P can cause the system to retract the previous consequence (S_t={P} becomes S_{t+1}={not-P}) -- structurally still U_NMR(S_t,E)->S_{t+1}, but not Bayesian posterior movement.

rationale_evidence.anchor: A1: Evidence supports P and A2: Evidence supports not-P. Argumentation theory can produce: arguments/attacks/defenses/accepted/rejected/undecided. rationale_evidence.statement: Argumentation theory instantiates U_R by producing arguments, attacks, defenses, and accepted/rejected/undecided classifications from conflicting evidence (A1 supports P, A2 supports not-P); the epistemic state S_t^arg is the accepted/defeated/undecided argument structure, updated as S_{t+1}^arg=U_arg(S_t,E) -- a representation very different from Bayesian probability but modelling the same kind of epistemic change.

rationale_evidence.anchor: K_a p means agent a knows p. M=(W,R_a,V) where W is a set of possible worlds. K_a p means p is true in all worlds accessible to a. So here S_t^EL is an epistemic possible-world structure. ... U_EL(S_t,E)->S_{t+1}. Same abstract role, different mathematics.
rationale_evidence.statement: Epistemic logic instantiates U_R via a possible-worlds model M=(W,R_a,V): K_a p (agent a knows p) means p is true in all worlds accessible to a; S_t^EL is an epistemic possible-world structure, updated as U_EL(S_t,E)->S_{t+1} -- same abstract role as other regimes, different mathematics.

rationale_evidence.anchor: G(P) meaning P is always true; F(P) meaning P will eventually become true. Now the epistemic state contains temporal properties ... Knows(a,p,t) and Valid(p,t). The temporal regime provides the semantics of how those evolve.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Roberts does not primarily tell us how to update knowledge. It asks: if we say some property of the epistemic state has a numerical value, is that number legitimate? ... f:R_emp->R that preserves the relevant structure. conceptual.anchor: What does it mean to have a complete or ideal state of an infinite Knowledge Space? ... 1. Explicit completeness -- impossible if the state is genuinely unbounded. 2. Structural completeness -- rules/relations are sufficient to derive answers. 3. Question-relative completeness -- sufficient to answer all questions in a defined question space. I suspect #2 and #3 will be much more important than #1 for KnowledgeOS.

formal.anchor: Human first has/conceives an Ideal State ... IDEAL STATE -> EXPECTATIONS/CRITERIA -> OBSERVATION -> COMPARISON -> DETERMINATION -> FACT/KNOWLEDGE. That is a substantially different model from the one I was using before.

governance.anchor: The object being observed and the process/actor observing it should not be conflated. ... separate bounded concepts such as: Observation, KnowledgeState, Evidence, Reasoning, Determination, Decision, Observer ... rather than one giant Knowledge aggregate.

rationale_evidence.anchor: P(A)=1, P(B)=0.9, P(C)=0.6, P(D)=0.2. Then our extracted representation of the ideal/current relationship is uncertain. The probability is therefore attached to the extraction/determination, not necessarily to the underlying ideal state itself. That gives: I_t -> hat-I_t where hat-I_t is probabilistically estimated from available information.
rationale_evidence.statement: Explains the origin of graded 0-to-1 values: if the ideal state requires A,B,C,D but observations only partially resolve them (P(A)=1,P(B)=0.9,P(C)=0.6,P(D)=0.2), the extracted representation of the ideal/current relationship is uncertain -- this probability attaches to the extraction/determination I_t -> hat-I_t, not to the underlying ideal state itself.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The word "old" is not an intrinsic property of version 2.69. It is a relational property: Old(2.69) iff 2.69 < ReferenceVersion_t. So if tomorrow the reference becomes 4.0, Old(2.69) remains true. But if the reference were somehow 2.0, Old(2.69) would be false.
rationale_evidence.statement: Establishes that 'old' is not an intrinsic property of a value but a relational property: Old(2.69) iff 2.69 < ReferenceVersion_t, whose truth depends entirely on the current reference (true if the reference rises to 4.0, false if the reference were 2.0) -- knowledge is often produced by comparing an observed state against a reference/ideal state, not by inspecting the observed state alone.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The ideal state itself is Knowledge. Someone had to establish: 3.85 is the current/required version. That did not come from the comparison. It came from another chain of knowledge: Vendor releases 3.85 -> Human/system observes it -> Evidence -> Determination -> "3.85 is current/required" -> Ideal/reference state. So KnowledgeOS has a recursive structure: Knowledge -> Ideal/Reference State -> Comparison -> New Knowledge.
rationale_evidence.statement: The ideal/reference state is itself Knowledge, established through its own prior chain (vendor releases 3.85 -> observed -> evidence -> determination -> '3.85 is current/required' -> becomes the ideal/reference state); this reveals KnowledgeOS has a recursive structure: Knowledge -> Ideal/Reference State -> Comparison -> New Knowledge -> (recursively) Updated Reference State -> ...

rationale_evidence.anchor: Many knowledge statements are not standalone facts. They are relationships between states. ... perhaps KnowledgeOS should not fundamentally think: Fact A, Fact B, Fact C but: Reference State <-> Observed State -> Comparison/Reasoning -> Determination.
rationale_evidence.statement: Argues many knowledge statements are relationships between states (2.69<3.85; CurrentArchitecture!=RequiredArchitecture; ObservedState does-not-entail RequiredState) rather than standalone facts; proposes KnowledgeOS should not fundamentally model Fact A/Fact B/Fact C as independent items, but as Reference State <-> Observed State -> Comparison/Reasoning -> Determination.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Knowledge at Monday and knowledge at Tuesday are different epistemic states. ... K_Monday -> K_Tuesday must preserve the trajectory. ... When a new dimension is discovered ... we gain knowledge. But the comparison with the previous state also reveals: The previous knowledge was less complete than today's knowledge. Even if the new dimension's value is known with 100% certainty.
rationale_evidence.statement: Knowledge at different times are different epistemic states, and a determination can be historically valid/obsolete/superseded/no longer applicable without deleting the historical record -- K_Monday -> K_Tuesday must preserve the trajectory. Also: discovering a new dimension retroactively reveals that the PREVIOUS knowledge state was less complete than today's, even when the new dimension's value is known with 100% certainty -- completeness assessment of past knowledge changes with later dimension discovery.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The reference itself has an epistemic history. We cannot simply store: RequiredVersion=3.85. We potentially need to know: Why do we accept 3.85 as the reference? ... Evidence -> Justification -> Trusted Statement -> Reference State -> Comparison -> New Determination. ... Trust is not the same as truth. ... Statement -> Reason -> Logic -> Justification -> Trust/Acceptance.
rationale_evidence.statement: The reference/ideal state is itself knowledge requiring its own epistemic history: not merely RequiredVersion=3.85, but why 3.85 is accepted (who stated it, what evidence/justification, what trust rule, when valid, who accepted it, has it since changed), giving the recursive chain Evidence -> Justification -> Trusted Statement -> Reference State -> Comparison -> New Determination. Trust is not the same as truth: a trusted source's statement must preserve why it is trusted (Statement -> Reason -> Logic -> Justification -> Trust/Acceptance), not merely who said it.

rationale_evidence.anchor: the ideal state exists independently of our knowledge. ... d_dependency in I_Mon even though humans do not know about it. So: Unknown dimension != Nonexistent dimension. ... Our observed state is only a projection. O_Mon = Pi(I_Mon | Information_Mon). ... the missing dimension is not a missing part of reality. It is a missing part of our observation/extraction. ... Discovery does not create the dimension. It changes our knowledge of the dimension. ... dimension discovery is an epistemic event, not an ontological event.
rationale_evidence.statement: Resolves an apparent reality/knowledge contradiction: the ideal state I_t exists independently of our knowledge of it -- a dependency dimension can already be an element of I_Mon (d_dependency in I_Mon) even though unknown, so unknown dimension != nonexistent dimension. The observed state is only a projection, O_Mon=Pi(I_Mon | Information_Mon), so a missing dimension is a gap in observation/extraction, not in reality. Discovery therefore does not create the dimension -- it changes our knowledge of it: dimension discovery is an epistemic event, not an ontological event.

rationale_evidence.anchor: How can we determine whether the new information changes the ideal state, or merely changes our knowledge of the already-existing ideal state? ... state change versus knowledge change ... one of the most important unresolved questions ... a Kernel that cannot distinguish those two will eventually corrupt the history of Knowledge. ... hat-I_Tue != hat-I_Mon even if none of the previously known values changed. ... both state and observed model of the state can change ... they are not mutually exclusive explanations.
rationale_evidence.statement: Distinguishes state change (the actual/ideal state I_t itself changes, e.g. Nexus is actually upgraded) from knowledge change (a previously-existing but unknown dimension is merely discovered) -- named one of the most important unresolved questions, since a Kernel unable to distinguish them will eventually corrupt the history of Knowledge. Formalizes that the observed ideal state must be recalculated purely from dimension-set expansion alone: if D_t subset D_{t+1}, then generally hat-I_t(D_t) != hat-I_{t+1}(D_{t+1}) even when every previously known dimension's value is unchanged -- the representation changed because the dimensional basis expanded, not because any value did. State change and dimension discovery can occur simultaneously and are not mutually exclusive explanations for why knowledge changed.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Truth(P)=1 while Determination(P)=? because nobody has discovered the evidence. This may be one of the most important foundational distinctions still missing.
rationale_evidence.statement: Argues Truth and Determination must be kept formally separate: a proposition can be true (Truth(P)=1) in reality while our Determination(P)=? because nobody has yet discovered the relevant evidence — flagged as possibly the most important missing foundational distinction in the whole model.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The object being observed and the process/actor observing it should not be conflated. ... separate bounded concepts such as: Observation, KnowledgeState, Evidence, Reasoning, Determination, Decision, Observer ... rather than one giant Knowledge aggregate.
rationale_evidence.statement: States a DDD architectural consequence: the observed object and the observing process/actor must not be conflated into one aggregate; proposes seven separate bounded concepts (Observation, KnowledgeState, Evidence, Reasoning, Determination, Decision, Observer) rather than one giant 'Knowledge' aggregate.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Arjuna's knowledge increases. He sees the people. But paradoxically, his certainty about what to do decreases. ... More information \not\Rightarrow More decision certainty ... KnowledgeOS should therefore never equate information volume with decision quality.
rationale_evidence.statement: Derives from Arjuna's crisis (more information about who he faces reduces, not increases, his certainty about what to do) the principle More information ⇏ More decision certainty, concluding KnowledgeOS must never equate information volume with decision quality — called one of the strongest observations in Chapter 1.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Sañjaya reports. He doesn't become Dhṛtarāṣṭra. ... KnowledgeOS should report, explain, challenge and expose—but the human remains the owner of understanding and decision. ... KnowledgeOS \neq DecisionOwner

Phase 1 (root, 99 docs) converged independently on Knowledge as a RELATIONSHIP, stated five times in one day across distinct documents (0135, 0225, 0249, 0302, 1057). Phase 2 (kernel, 151 docs) shifted to a factive, participant-relative, time-dependent relation directed at a Knowledge Space, adding two conceptions absent from Phase 1: capacity and measure-over-a-space. Correction: the relationship conception is Phase 1 original project thinking, not an import from later book-derived research; conversely Knowledge Space (Phase 2 sense), capacity, and measure must not be attributed to Phase 1.

rationale_evidence.statement: Eleven competing conceptions of knowledge, all preserved and none chosen: K-1 stored content/a thing (rejected by both corpus and formal law); K-2 a justified/governed relationship among knower/object/evidence/reasoning/context/conclusion (Phase 1 original, dominant P1 position); K-3 justified state evolution (Phase 1 original); K-4 not one entity — an epistemic pipeline (Phase 1 original); K-5 Cognitive Worlds space partition (Phase 1, book-derived, never developed further); K-6 factive/participant-relative/time-dependent relation to a Knowledge Space (Phase 2, Gelfond & Kahl-derived); K-7 a capacity to project/discriminate/select/decide (Phase 2, response-mode); K-8 continuously changing body/dynamic flow (Phase 2, response-mode); K-9 structured state in a measurable space, projection as measure (Phase 2 architectural proposal, directly attacked by 181719=S0569); K-10 institutional/social, not individual (Phase 2, Searle-derived); K-11 primitive and unanalysable (Phase 2, Williamson-derived) — the deepest tension, since it denies the whole definitional field rather than competing within it; no document reconciles K-11 with K-2..K-9.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Phase 1 asked *what knowledge consists of*; Phase 2 asked *what knowledge is relative to* — a space, a participant, a time.

What changed: the relatum moved from an internal list (reality/observer/evidence/reasoning) to an external space. What did not change: the refusal of stored content, the corpus's most stable result across both phases, agreeing with formal law §17. Self-correction: an earlier claim that 'Knowledge Space' first appears at kernel/20260825-103542 was kernel-scoped and wrong corpus-wide — the phrase appears three days earlier at 20260822-0200 (Phase 1) as a diagram label for 'Cognitive Worlds' explaining why contradictions can coexist, but it is a different concept (no unboundedness, no projection, no participant relativity, no time index) — restated as 'same term, different concept', not 'term absent.'

rationale_evidence.statement: Four competing identity positions found: identity assigned-never-derived (formal law INV-KOS-IDENTITY-001, echoed by corpus, both phases); identity primitive/unitary/indefinable (McGinn, kernel 115235/120122, Phase 2 book); identity transformational/contextual (Daoist ziran, kernel 094638, Phase 2 book, 170 references, the only K4-strength challenge); identity relational — since knowledge IS the relationship, identity is the relation's (0135, 0225, Phase 1 original). Asymmetry noted: the only K4-strength challenge to identity is book-derived while the position it attacks is constitutional; no Phase 1 document takes a position on the nature of identity (P1 treats identity as needed, not explained). 'Can knowledge exist without identity?' is not addressed anywhere in the corpus; formal law answers by construction (removing identity makes the system 'a document store, an embedding database, or a similarity engine').

rationale_evidence.statement: 42 Phase 2 documents carry temporal material versus almost none in Phase 1 ('at time t' appears once in the 13 earliest kernel documents and is rare at root). Positions: knowledge inherently knowledge-at-a-time (Phase 2 only, 171853/171008); knowledge revisable but not intrinsically temporal (Phase 1, 0302); knowledge evolves through governed transitions (Phase 1, 1016/1018); change is continuous (Phase 2, 160637/135642). 'Does change create a new identity?' is asked and answered by no document — the sharpest unresolved temporal question, exactly where K-8 (continuous change) and formal law (forward-only governed transitions, nothing overwritten) would collide; formal law's 'a revision creates a new state and retains the prior one' answers state succession, not identity succession.

But 'factive' (K-6, from Williamson via Gelfond & Kahl chain) reintroduces truth by the back door: a factive relation entails truth, yet a system with no access to truth cannot verify factivity — this tension is unreconciled, and is flagged as the same defect class previously recorded against possible-worlds π.

rationale_evidence.anchor: K-4, K-7 and K-9 **cannot support an identity-bearing aggregate at all**. If any of them were true, the current core domain (*Knowledge Identity*) would have no object.
rationale_evidence.statement: DDD boundary implications table across six conceptions: K-2 relationship -> identity belongs to the relation, admission=establishing a relatum set; K-3 state evolution -> identity assigned/persistent, admission=a governed transition; K-4 pipeline -> nothing single bears identity, identity undefined; K-6 factive relation to a space -> participant-indexed identity, admission requires truth access; K-7 capacity -> not storable, a capacity has no record; K-9 measure -> a measure/distribution, measures lack identity. Sharpest observation: K-4 (pipeline), K-7 (capacity), and K-9 (measure) cannot support an identity-bearing aggregate at all — if any were true, the current formal core domain (Knowledge Identity) would have no object, making them the corpus's most consequential falsification candidates; none of the three is Phase 1 (original project thinking).
